May to Sep 2026MA dissertation

The Localization Playbook: how six luxury houses speak to the Gulf

Louis Vuitton, Dior, Chanel, Cartier, Bvlgari and Hermès all adapt for Saudi Arabia and the UAE. The real story is that they don't do it equally in public.

Data
9,625 Instagram posts
Markets
Saudi Arabia and UAE
Period
Jan 2022 to Jun 2026
  1. None of the brands speak to their established Arabic-speaking audience in Arabic on their main feeds.
  2. Louis Vuitton regularly uses oud and desert imagery without ever linking it to the Gulf.
  3. LV's Gulf capsule, Mirage, launched in January 2026. LV posted 67 times that month and none of the posts mentioned it.
  4. Chanel made a major retail investment in Riyadh with zero disclosure on its feed.
See the framework and recommendationsClose

I tested each brand against Kapferer and Bastien's anti-laws of luxury, using a six-brand case study and a netnography of their global Instagram feeds. The contribution is a simple idea the literature hadn't drawn: Audience Direction, the difference between a brand speaking to a region and a region simply seeing global content. Crossed with three levels of localisation, it makes this matrix:

The Localisation Diagnostic by Audience Direction (Figure 12 of the dissertation). Chanel sits outside the matrix because its Gulf activity doesn't appear on its public feed.
Market-directedGlobally directed
Aesthetic hybridityNo clear caseDior, by character: signal concentrated in one November 2024 exhibition
Symbolic accommodationBvlgari (most secure), Cartier, Dior (by count), Hermès (lowest intensity)No case
Surface exploitationNo caseLouis Vuitton: 24 motif posts, zero regional address

My recommendations: bring Arabic onto main feeds, name the cultures being borrowed from, explain silence where a brand is investing heavily, keep regional campaigns on the main account, treat Saudi Arabia and the UAE as separate markets, and read Arabic and Arabizi comments as audience data. With Vision 2030's creative economy push, local partnerships and direct address are also the more sustainable route.

Bremont: a 2027 campaign in three acts

A consultancy brief for the British watchmaker, built around the Terra Nova collection and a new Wayfinder identity, and designed to fix retention as much as acquisition.

Budget
£3.2M over 12 months
Markets
US and UK
Delivered
Report and pitch deck
Read the full projectClose
  • Act 001, The Exhibit. Heritage installations at Heathrow, JFK, Grand Central and Waterloo: wartime aircraft in glass cases alongside Terra Nova watches.
  • Act 002, The Collective. A travelling pop-up across New York, Miami, Dallas and Los Angeles with Aston Martin, Hackett London, Crockett & Jones and Globe-Trotter.
  • Act 003, The Wayfinder Weekends. A members-only outdoor programme for Bremont owners, led by adventurers and mountaineers.

Grounded in Pine & Gilmore's Experience Economy and Moore's brand ecosystem theory.

Mar to May 2026Exploring the Language of Display

Hana to Heiwa at Mitsukoshi Nihonbashi

"Flowers and Peace": a six-day display event for the Tokyo flagship, running from Hinamatsuri to International Women's Day 2027, telling a political story through space instead of slogans.

Place
Tokyo
Length
Six days
Concept partners
Issey Miyake, Mikimoto, Wajima lacquer

Concept illustrations by me, made with AI assistance.

Read the full projectClose
Display is treated as a message, not simply as décor.

Visitors move from a chrysanthemum facade to a hinadan in the Central Hall beneath the 1930 pipe organ, then to a Leadership Gallery ending at an empty plinth labelled "2027". A corridor of tsurushi-bina hanging dolls, paper cranes and cherry blossom runs from cosmetics to jewellery.

The work covered the facade, three interior zones, brand collaborations, a PR plan with Tokyo Metro posters, press invitations and social tiles, and staff styling.

Nov 2025 to Jan 2026Principles of Luxury

Cagliostro: a cigar house for those who command the room

A luxury brand I built from nothing, named after an 18th-century magician who captivated high society: identity, four collections, a website, an Instagram plan and a brand film concept.

Read the full projectClose

Cagliostro runs on what I called a "digital velvet rope": holding information back on purpose, so the brand stays a little out of reach. It draws on Kapferer's anti-laws, Veblen and Bourdieu.

The four collections are Signature, Grand Cru, Aniversario and Millennium, each with its own character, from creamy to intense.

Oct 2025 to Jan 2026Professional Luxury Practices

Fabergé: a recovery plan for the Tsar's jeweller

A business report on Fabergé under Gemfields ownership, with a three-part strategy for 2026 to 2030.

2024 revenue
USD 13.4M
Operating loss
USD 5.7M
Read the full projectClose

Fabergé has imperial heritage and direct access to responsibly sourced coloured gemstones. By 2024 it also faced falling revenue and customers asking "is this the real Fabergé?"

  • Financial focus: selective divestment and leaner operations.
  • Brand clarity: experiential retail and private client work in key cities.
  • Provenance: blockchain-backed tracking and imperial storytelling for buyers who want ethical, meaningful luxury.
Nov 2025 to Jan 2026Context of Luxury

Why is luxury a contested issue?

An essay on class, identity and menswear, from Beau Brummell and the Teddy Boys to Virgil Abloh at Louis Vuitton.

Read the summaryClose

Using Bourdieu's habitus and cultural capital, the essay follows how luxury has marked class, and how Gen Z values and Abloh's "zeroing" approach unsettled that. It ends on quiet luxury: rejecting logos is still a way of signalling status, just a quieter one.

Luxury is not simply a category of goods. It is a symbolic system through which social hierarchies are reproduced, disrupted and renegotiated. From my MA essay, Why is luxury a contested issue?

A little about me

I grew up in Pakistan, studied business in Lahore, and came to Southampton to study luxury properly. What keeps me interested is the gap between how a brand sees itself and how a customer actually receives it.

My CRM work sits on the customer side of that gap, and my MA sat on the brand side. I'd like my next role to connect the two, whether that's in CRM, brand or client marketing.

I'm based in the North West of England and happy to move, including to London or Dubai.
